subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Hawking Radiation
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Hawking Radiation.

hook.text: Black holes aren't truly black. Stephen Hawking predicted in 1974 that they slowly emit radiation and shrink.

buildup.text: Near the event horizon, quantum fluctuations create particle-antiparticle pairs. One falls in, the other escapes.

discovery.text: The escaping particles carry away energy, causing the black hole to lose mass over time. It's evaporating.

twist.text: For stellar black holes, evaporation takes longer than the age of the universe. They're effectively permanent—for now.

climax.text: Hawking radiation has never been directly observed. Confirming it would be a landmark in quantum gravity.

punchline.text: Even black holes die. They just take longer than everything else.

quiz.question: What causes Hawking radiation?
options: Quantum particle pairs form near the horizon; one escapes while the other falls in
The black hole's magnetic field ejects charged particles
Light trapped inside slowly leaks out through cracks in the event horizon

details.summary: Stephen Hawking predicted in 1974 that black holes aren't truly black — quantum effects near the event horizon cause them to emit faint thermal radiation, slowly losing mass.
details.whyItMatters: Hawking radiation was the first theoretical result linking quantum mechanics, thermodynamics, and gravity. It implies black holes have a temperature, an entropy, and a finite lifetime — revolutionizing theoretical physics.
takeaways: Quantum effects cause black holes to emit faint radiation
Black holes slowly lose mass and eventually evaporate
The discovery linked quantum mechanics to gravity

faq.question: Has Hawking radiation been detected?
faq.answer: No. For stellar-mass black holes, the radiation is unimaginably faint — far below any detector's sensitivity. The temperature of a solar-mass black hole is about 60 nanokelvins, colder than the cosmic microwave background. Only microscopic black holes would radiate detectably.

faq.question: How long does black hole evaporation take?
faq.answer: A stellar-mass black hole would take roughly 10^67 years to evaporate — trillions of trillions of times longer than the current age of the universe. Supermassive black holes would take 10^100 years. Only microscopic black holes could evaporate on observable timescales.
